title: Prompting & Structured Outputs
summary: A language model produces text. Your program needs data. This module is about closing that gap reliably, not with a nicer-sounding prompt, but with validation and repair logic that doesn't trust the model to behave.
objectives: Explain why raw model output is not a data format, and where that assumption breaks production systems
Design a prompt with a clear role, instructions, and few-shot examples that reduce output variance
Detect and repair the most common malformed-output patterns (code fences, trailing commas, extra prose)
Implement a real validator that checks output against a schema before your program trusts it

lessons.title: The gap between "sounds right" and "is data"
Few-shot examples reduce variance, not risk to zero
Before the checkpoint: what you should now be able to do

exercise.label: Code exercise · Python, runs in a real sandboxed Python interpreter (Pyodide)
exercise.instructions: Complete `extract_structured_output(raw_text, schema)`. `schema` is a dict `{"required": [...]}`, the list of field names that must be present. Return `{"ok": True, "data": ...}` on success, or `{"ok": False, "error": ...}` on failure, where `error` is a short human-readable string. Handle: markdown code fences around the JSON, a trailing comma before `}` or `]`, and a missing required field. Never raise, always return one of the two shapes above, even for completely non-JSON input.
exercise.starter:
import json
import re

def extract_structured_output(raw_text, schema):
    # Handle: markdown code fences, a trailing comma, and a missing required field.
    # Return {"ok": True, "data": ...} or {"ok": False, "error": ...}. Never raise.

    # YOUR CODE HERE

    pass

hints.title: Hint 1 — conceptual
hints.mdx: Think in three passes: (1) clean up formatting noise around the JSON, (2) try to parse it, (3) check the parsed dict actually has what you need. Each pass can fail independently, and each failure should produce a useful error, not a raised exception.

hints.title: Hint 2 — specific
hints.mdx: Python's `re` module: ````re.match(r"^```(?:json)?\s*([\s\S]*?)\s*```$", text)```` captures the content between fences. For trailing commas, `re.sub(r",\s*([}\]])", r"\1", text)` before parsing. Wrap `json.loads` in try/except, don't let it raise out of your function.

hints.title: Hint 3 — near-solution
hints.mdx: After a successful parse, loop over `schema.get("required", [])` and check `field in data` for each one. Return a specific error naming the missing field on the first one that's absent, don't just say "invalid".

tests.name: Alice
tests.hint: A well-formed JSON string matching the schema should return {"ok": True, "data": ...} with the parsed values intact.

tests.name: Priya
tests.hint: Strip a leading/trailing ``` (optionally ```json) fence before attempting json.loads.

tests.name: Alex
tests.hint: Replace a comma immediately before a closing } or ] with nothing before parsing.

tests.name: Sam
tests.hint: After parsing, check every field in schema["required"] is present, and name the missing one in the error.

tests.name: Non-JSON prose is rejected gracefully, not raised
tests.hint: Wrap json.loads in try/except, plain prose will raise json.JSONDecodeError, catch it and return {"ok": False, "error": ...}.

questions.question: A model is instructed "respond only with valid JSON, no other text" and given two examples. What should a production system still do with its response?

options.text: Validate and parse it before trusting it, exactly as if it came from any other untrusted external source
options.why: Treat model output like any other untrusted input, validate before use.

options.text: Trust it directly, the instruction plus examples make malformed output effectively impossible
options.why: Instructions and examples reduce the RATE of malformed output, they don't reduce it to zero, a production system still needs to validate.

options.text: Log a warning but proceed with whatever text came back
options.why: Logging a warning after already acting on unvalidated data doesn't prevent the corruption or crash that malformed data can cause, validation has to happen before use, not after.

questions.principle: Treat model output like any other untrusted input, validate before use.

questions.question: Where does a standing output-format instruction (e.g. "always respond in JSON") most reliably belong?

options.text: The system role, stated once, reinforced with an example
options.why: The system role is for standing instructions that apply across the whole conversation.

options.text: Anywhere in the user message, position doesn't matter
options.why: Position does matter in practice, instructions buried mid-message compete with the actual request for the model's attention, a standing instruction belongs in the system role.

options.text: It should be repeated in every assistant turn instead of stated once
options.why: A standing instruction doesn't need to be repeated every turn if it's placed in the system role, that's exactly what the system role is for, persistent instructions that apply for the whole conversation.

questions.principle: The system role is for standing instructions that apply across the whole conversation.

questions.question: A response is `{"name": "Sam"}`, syntactically valid JSON, but your schema requires `age` too. Is this a repair-pass issue or a validation issue?

options.text: Validation, the JSON is syntactically fine, the repair pass has nothing to fix
options.why: Syntactically valid but semantically incomplete is a validation problem, not a repair-pass problem.

options.text: Repair pass, this is exactly what stripping trailing commas is for
options.why: There's no syntax problem here to repair, {"name": "Sam"} parses successfully, the issue is that the resulting DATA is incomplete, which is what validation checks for, not the repair pass.

options.text: Neither, this response should be accepted as-is
options.why: The response is missing a field your schema explicitly requires, accepting it as-is means your program later fails (or behaves wrong) when it tries to use the missing age field.

questions.principle: Syntactically valid but semantically incomplete is a validation problem, not a repair-pass problem.

questions.question: Why do few-shot examples typically improve output consistency more than a longer text description of the desired format?

options.text: A concrete example removes ambiguity a prose description leaves open (nesting, extra fields, exact key names)
options.why: Concrete examples remove interpretive ambiguity that prose descriptions leave open.

options.text: Examples make the prompt longer, and longer prompts are always more reliable
options.why: Length itself isn't what helps, a long, vague description doesn't outperform a short, concrete example. It's the removal of ambiguity that matters, not the character count.

options.text: Examples let the model skip following the system instructions entirely
options.why: Examples work alongside the system instructions, reinforcing them concretely, they don't replace or let the model ignore those instructions.

questions.principle: Concrete examples remove interpretive ambiguity that prose descriptions leave open.

questions.question: A response comes back as: ```` ```json\n{"status": "ok",}\n``` ````. After stripping the code fence and the trailing comma, is the remaining text valid JSON?

options.why: Correct. After stripping the fence and the trailing comma, the remaining text is {"status": "ok"}, which is valid JSON.
Not quite. After stripping the ``` fence and the trailing comma before }, what's left is {"status": "ok"}, which IS valid JSON, that's exactly why the repair pass runs before parsing.

glossary.definition: model output constrained to a predictable, parseable shape, typically JSON.
including example input/output pairs in the prompt to demonstrate the desired response shape.
the three message roles most model APIs use to separate standing instructions, the current request, and prior responses.
deterministic cleanup (stripping fences, trailing commas) attempted before treating a response as unparseable.
checking that successfully-parsed data actually contains the fields a consumer requires.
